description: Build a budget from zero each period. Every dollar must be justified by its expected return, not by the fact that it was spent last period. Forces conscious allocation instead of inertial spending. Works for households, departments, and entire organizations.

steps.description: Start from zero. List every category of spending with last period's amount, then set each to zero. The burden of proof is on the spending, not on the cut.

inputs.name: last-period-spending
inputs.desc: All spending from the previous period, categorized

inputs.name: available-funds
inputs.desc: Total funds available for the upcoming period

outputs.name: spending-categories
outputs.desc: Every category with its last-period amount and a zero starting point

outputs.name: total-available
outputs.desc: The total funds to allocate from zero

process: Export the previous period's spending by category. Include fixed obligations (rent, insurance, loan payments) and variable spending (marketing, supplies, entertainment, subscriptions).
Set every category to zero. The previous amount is reference data, not a starting point. Each category must earn its allocation from scratch.
Separate non-negotiable obligations (contractual commitments that cannot be reduced this period) from discretionary spending. Non-negotiable amounts are allocated first.
Calculate the remaining pool after non-negotiable allocations. This is the amount available for discretionary allocation.

steps.description: For each discretionary category, build the justification: what value does this spending produce, and what evidence supports the claim?

outputs.name: justified-requests
outputs.desc: Each category with its requested amount, the expected return, and the evidence supporting the return estimate

outputs.name: unjustified-spending
outputs.desc: Categories where no clear return could be articulated, candidates for elimination

process: For each discretionary category, answer three questions: What does this spending produce? How do we know? What happens if we cut it to zero?

Quantify the expected return where possible. Marketing: expected revenue attributed. Training: skill gap closed. Subscriptions: hours saved per month. If you cannot quantify it, describe the qualitative impact and rate its importance.
For categories where the return is unclear or unmeasured, flag them as unjustified. These are the first candidates for reduction or elimination.
Rank the justified requests by return on investment: expected return divided by requested amount. The highest-ROI categories get funded first.

steps.description: Allocate funds in priority order until the pool is exhausted. The last funded category is the marginal allocation. Everything below it is unfunded.

outputs.name: funded-categories
outputs.desc: Each funded category with its allocated amount and the running total

outputs.name: unfunded-categories
outputs.desc: Categories that did not make the cut, with the amount they requested

outputs.name: marginal-allocation
outputs.desc: The last funded category: the one at the boundary between funded and unfunded

process: Starting with the highest-ROI category, allocate its requested amount. Subtract from the pool. Move to the next category.
Continue until the pool is exhausted. The last category that fits is the marginal allocation. Everything below it is unfunded for this period.
If a category's full request does not fit, consider partial funding: can the category produce a proportional return at a reduced level?
The unfunded list is not waste. It is the waiting list. If any funded category underperforms, the top unfunded category gets its allocation.

steps.description: Set up variance tracking: actual spending vs. allocated amount for each category. Variances trigger reallocation decisions, not just reports.

outputs.name: variance-tracking-plan
outputs.desc: For each category: the allocated amount, the tracking frequency, and the variance threshold that triggers review

outputs.name: reallocation-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for reallocating funds: underspend in one category can fund the top unfunded category

process: For each funded category, set the tracking frequency: weekly for high-velocity spending (variable costs, marketing), monthly for stable spending (subscriptions, fixed costs).
Set the variance threshold: a deviation of more than 15% from the allocated amount triggers a review. The review asks: is the variance a timing issue or a structural issue?
Define the reallocation rules: if a category is trending to underspend by more than 20%, the excess can be reallocated to the highest-priority unfunded category.
At the end of the period, the variance data becomes the evidence base for the next zero-based cycle.

steps.description: Review the zero-based budget at period end. Compare actual returns to justified estimates. Categories that delivered less than promised lose credibility in the next cycle.

inputs.name: variance-tracking-plan
inputs.desc: The tracking setup and actual variances

inputs.name: justified-requests
inputs.desc: The original justifications with expected returns

outputs.name: return-scorecard
outputs.desc: Each category's promised return vs. actual return, with a credibility rating for the next cycle

outputs.name: next-cycle-inputs
outputs.desc: The spending data, return data, and credibility ratings that feed the next zero-based cycle

process: For each funded category, compare the actual return to the justified estimate. Calculate the accuracy: actual divided by estimated.
Categories that consistently overestimate their returns lose credibility. In the next cycle, their estimates are discounted by their historical accuracy rate.
Categories that consistently deliver are trusted. Their estimates carry full weight in the next cycle.
Feed the scorecard into the next zero-based cycle. The discipline improves over time as estimate accuracy is tracked and calibrated.

description: Determine where the next dollar produces the most value. Marginal analysis asks: given that I am already spending X, what is the return on one more dollar in each category? The answer is almost never the same as the average return. Use for household spending decisions, marketing budget allocation, hiring decisions, and investment choices.

steps.description: Capture the current allocation across all spending categories and the current return from each.

inputs.name: spending-categories
inputs.desc: All categories where money is currently allocated

inputs.name: return-metrics
inputs.desc: The measurable return from each category (revenue, savings, satisfaction, time recovered)

outputs.name: allocation-snapshot
outputs.desc: Each category with its current spend and current measured return

outputs.name: average-returns
outputs.desc: The average return per dollar for each category (total return divided by total spend)

process: List every spending category with the current period's allocation and the measured return.
Calculate the average return per dollar: total return from the category divided by total spend. This is the number most people use to allocate, and it is the wrong number.

Note the limitation: average return tells you what the existing dollars produce. It does not tell you what the next dollar would produce. A category with high average returns may have declining marginal returns.
Flag categories where you have no data on returns. These are blind spots that need measurement before marginal analysis can include them.

steps.description: Estimate the marginal return: what one additional dollar (or unit of resource) would produce in each category, given current spending levels.

inputs.name: average-returns
inputs.desc: The average return per dollar for reference

outputs.name: marginal-returns
outputs.desc: For each category: the estimated return from one additional dollar, with the reasoning and evidence

outputs.name: diminishing-return-flags
outputs.desc: Categories where marginal returns are significantly lower than average returns, indicating diminishing returns

process: For each category, estimate the marginal return by asking: if I increase spending by 10%, what incremental return do I expect? Divide the incremental return by the incremental spend.
Look for diminishing returns: categories where the marginal return is less than 50% of the average return. These are saturated. More spending produces less and less.

Look for increasing returns: categories where the marginal return exceeds the average. These are underfunded. More spending produces accelerating results (common in early-stage marketing or network-effect products).

Where historical data exists (last quarter you increased spend by X and got Y more return), use it. Where it does not, estimate based on the mechanism: is there a logical reason more spending would produce more return?

steps.description: Find reallocation opportunities: move dollars from categories with low marginal returns to categories with high marginal returns.

inputs.name: marginal-returns
inputs.desc: The marginal return estimates for each category

outputs.name: reallocation-opportunities
outputs.desc: Pairs of categories: take from the low-marginal-return category, give to the high-marginal-return category, with the expected net gain

outputs.name: reallocation-constraints
outputs.desc: Minimum spending levels below which a category cannot function (the floor), preventing over-optimization

process: Rank categories by marginal return, highest to lowest. The spread between the highest and lowest marginal returns is your reallocation opportunity.
For each low-marginal-return category, determine the floor: the minimum spend below which the category cannot function. You can take from above the floor but not below it.
Pair the highest-marginal-return categories (destinations) with the lowest-marginal-return categories (sources). Calculate the net gain: marginal return gained minus marginal return lost.
Prioritize reallocations by net gain. The highest-net-gain reallocation is the single best move you can make with your existing budget.

steps.description: Apply marginal analysis to the specific decision: should I spend more, spend less, or reallocate? The framework applies to any resource decision.

outputs.name: spending-decisions
outputs.desc: For each category: increase, decrease, hold, or reallocate, with the specific amount and the expected impact

outputs.name: marginal-analysis-document
outputs.desc: The complete analysis: current allocation, marginal returns, reallocation opportunities, and decisions

process: For each category, apply the decision rule: if marginal return exceeds the cost of capital (or the opportunity cost of the next-best use), increase spending. If it is below, decrease.
Where the marginal return equals the opportunity cost, you are at the optimal allocation for that category. Hold.
Execute the reallocations in order of net gain. After each reallocation, re-estimate the marginal returns (they change as spending levels change).
Document the analysis and the decisions. Set the re-analysis frequency: monthly for high-velocity categories, quarterly for stable ones.

description: Apply the Theory of Constraints to resource allocation. Find the bottleneck that limits the system's output. Allocate resources to exploit the bottleneck first, then subordinate everything else to it. Adding resources anywhere except the bottleneck is waste.

steps.description: Identify the bottleneck: the single resource, process, or capacity constraint that limits the entire system's throughput.

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: The system to optimize (a production process, a sales funnel, a household schedule, a project pipeline)

inputs.name: throughput-goal
inputs.desc: The desired output of the system per time period

outputs.name: bottleneck-identification
outputs.desc: The single constraint that limits throughput, with the evidence (the step where work queues up, the resource that is at 100% utilization, the process with the longest cycle time)

outputs.name: system-flow-map
outputs.desc: The sequence of steps from input to output with the capacity and utilization of each

process: Map the system from input to output. For each step: what is the capacity (units per time period) and what is the current utilization (actual output divided by capacity)?
The bottleneck is the step with the highest utilization. If one step is at 95% and all others are at 60%, the 95% step is the bottleneck. Work queues up before it and everything after it is starved.
Verify by asking: if I could increase this step's capacity by 10%, would the system's total output increase? If yes, it is the bottleneck. If no, you identified the wrong step.
There is always exactly one bottleneck at any given time. If you see two, one of them is hiding a buffer.

steps.description: Exploit the bottleneck: make sure it is never idle, never processing low-value work, and never doing anything that a non-bottleneck resource could do instead.

outputs.name: exploitation-plan
outputs.desc: Actions to get more throughput from the bottleneck without adding resources: eliminate idle time, prioritize high-value work, offload non-bottleneck tasks

outputs.name: expected-throughput-gain
outputs.desc: The estimated increase in system throughput from exploitation alone

process: Audit the bottleneck's time: how much is productive (processing the highest-value work), how much is idle (waiting for inputs, changeover, maintenance), and how much is low-value (processing work that should go elsewhere)?
Eliminate idle time: ensure the bottleneck always has a queue of ready work. Buffer the input so the bottleneck never waits.
Prioritize the bottleneck's work: process the highest-value items first. Low-value work that uses bottleneck capacity is the most expensive waste in the system.
Offload anything the bottleneck does that a non-bottleneck could do. If the bottleneck does setup, inspection, or admin that could be done by a less constrained resource, move it.

steps.description: Subordinate everything else to the bottleneck's pace. Non-bottleneck resources should produce only what the bottleneck can process. Overproduction before the bottleneck creates inventory; underproduction starves it.

outputs.name: subordination-rules
outputs.desc: For each non-bottleneck step: the production rate to match the bottleneck's pace, and the buffer size to maintain

outputs.name: resource-liberation
outputs.desc: Resources freed by slowing non-bottleneck steps to the bottleneck's pace, available for reallocation

process: Set each non-bottleneck step's production rate to match the bottleneck's throughput. Producing faster than the bottleneck can process creates waste (inventory, overwork, context switching).
Place a buffer before the bottleneck (to prevent starvation) and after it (to protect downstream from bottleneck variability). Size the buffers to cover the bottleneck's cycle time variability.
Identify the resources freed by subordination: if a non-bottleneck step was running at 90% but only needs to run at 60%, the difference is available for other uses.
Resist the temptation to keep non-bottleneck resources busy with non-essential work. Idle time at a non-bottleneck is free. Idle time at the bottleneck is the system's most expensive waste.

steps.description: If exploitation and subordination are not enough, elevate the bottleneck: add capacity through investment. Only invest after exploitation and subordination have been exhausted.

outputs.name: elevation-options
outputs.desc: Options to increase the bottleneck's capacity: additional resources, technology, outsourcing, process redesign, with cost and expected throughput gain for each

outputs.name: elevation-decision
outputs.desc: The selected option with the investment amount and the payback period (throughput gain times value per unit divided by investment cost)

process: List the options to increase the bottleneck's capacity: hire another person, buy another machine, outsource the step, redesign the process, add a shift.
For each option, estimate the cost and the throughput gain. Calculate the payback: how many periods until the increased throughput revenue exceeds the investment?
Select the option with the shortest payback. If no option has an acceptable payback, the system's throughput is capped at the current bottleneck capacity.
After elevation, re-identify the bottleneck. It will have moved to a different step. The new bottleneck is now the constraint, and the cycle begins again.

steps.description: Track the constraint cycle over time. As bottlenecks are elevated, new ones emerge. The cycle never ends. The system improves by working the constraint cycle faster, not by reaching a state without constraints.

inputs.name: elevation-decision
inputs.desc: The investment made to elevate the bottleneck

outputs.name: constraint-cycle-log
outputs.desc: The history of bottleneck identifications, exploitations, subordinations, and elevations, with the throughput gain at each step

outputs.name: current-bottleneck-report
outputs.desc: The current bottleneck, its utilization, and the next exploitation opportunity

process: Log the constraint cycle: when was each bottleneck identified, what was done to exploit and subordinate it, when was it elevated, and what throughput gain resulted?
After each elevation, immediately re-identify the new bottleneck. Do not assume: measure utilization at every step.
Compare the system's throughput over time. Each constraint cycle should produce a measurable throughput increase. If it does not, the exploitation or subordination was incomplete.
Set the review cadence: weekly bottleneck check (has it moved?), monthly exploitation review (are we getting everything from it?), quarterly elevation review (should we invest?).

description: Optimize the timing of cash inflows and outflows. The total amount matters less than when it arrives and when it leaves. A business (or household) that collects before it pays has free float. One that pays before it collects needs financing. Map every inflow and outflow to a calendar, find the gaps, and close them.

steps.description: Map every expected inflow and outflow to a calendar. Daily resolution for the next 90 days, weekly for the next 6 months, monthly for the next year.

inputs.name: income-sources
inputs.desc: All sources of inflow with amounts, frequency, and typical timing (e.g., client pays on net-30, salary hits on the 15th and 30th)

inputs.name: expense-obligations
inputs.desc: All outflows with amounts, frequency, and due dates

outputs.name: cash-flow-calendar
outputs.desc: A day-by-day projection of the bank balance: starting balance, plus inflows, minus outflows, equals ending balance for each day

outputs.name: negative-balance-days
outputs.desc: Any day where the projected balance goes below zero or below the minimum reserve threshold

process: List every inflow: when does it typically arrive (not when it is invoiced, but when the cash hits the account)? Account for payment delays. If a client is on net-30 terms but historically pays on day 45, use day 45.
List every outflow: when is it due, and when does it actually leave the account (auto-pay dates, check clearing delays)?
Build the calendar: starting balance on day 1, add inflows, subtract outflows, calculate the running balance for each day.
Mark the days where the balance drops below zero or below the minimum reserve. These are the cash flow gaps that need to be addressed.

steps.description: Close cash flow gaps by adjusting timing: accelerate inflows, decelerate outflows, or both.

inputs.name: negative-balance-days
inputs.desc: The days with cash flow gaps

outputs.name: timing-adjustments
outputs.desc: Specific changes to close each gap: invoice earlier, offer early-payment discounts, negotiate longer payment terms, batch payments to match inflow timing

outputs.name: revised-calendar
outputs.desc: The updated cash flow calendar with the timing adjustments applied

process: For each gap, identify the cause: is the gap caused by a delayed inflow (client pays late), a lumpy outflow (annual insurance premium), or a structural mismatch (you pay suppliers before customers pay you)?
Accelerate inflows: invoice immediately instead of at month-end, offer a 2% discount for payment within 10 days, require deposits for large projects, switch from net-60 to net-30 terms.
Decelerate outflows: negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers, batch discretionary payments to align with inflow timing, switch annual payments to monthly (if the annualized cost is acceptable).
Rebuild the calendar with the adjustments. If gaps remain, they must be covered by a line of credit or reserve draw.

steps.description: Maximize the float: the period between collecting and paying. Float is free financing. The goal is to collect as early as possible and pay as late as allowed.

inputs.name: income-sources
inputs.desc: The inflow sources and their terms

outputs.name: float-analysis
outputs.desc: The average float in days (weighted by amount) and the interest or investment income the float generates

outputs.name: float-improvement-plan
outputs.desc: Actions to extend the float: earlier collection, later payment, higher-yield sweep accounts

process: Calculate the average float: for each dollar, how many days does it sit in your account between collection and disbursement? Weight by amount.
For the float period, determine where the cash sits. If it is in a zero-interest checking account, the float generates nothing. Move it to a high-yield sweep account or money market fund.
Identify float extension opportunities: can collection be moved earlier without losing customers? Can payment be moved later without losing vendor goodwill or triggering penalties?
Calculate the annual value of the float: average float balance times the yield rate. Even small yields on large floats produce meaningful returns.

steps.description: Stress-test the cash flow: what happens if the largest inflow is delayed by 30 days, or two major outflows hit simultaneously?

outputs.name: stress-scenarios
outputs.desc: Three stress scenarios (delayed inflow, accelerated outflow, combined) with the resulting cash position over 90 days

outputs.name: contingency-triggers
outputs.desc: The balance thresholds that trigger each contingency action: draw reserves, activate credit line, defer discretionary spending, accelerate collections

process: Scenario 1: the largest single inflow is delayed by 30 days. What is the lowest point in the cash balance? Can you survive without additional financing?
Scenario 2: two of the three largest outflows hit in the same week (insurance renewal plus tax payment, or two vendor invoices plus payroll). What is the lowest point?
Scenario 3: both happen simultaneously. This is the worst plausible case.

For each scenario, define the contingency trigger: at what balance level do you draw reserves, activate a credit line, defer discretionary spending, or accelerate collections? Write the triggers before the stress happens, not during.

description: Make the hidden cost of every decision visible. Every time you allocate a resource (money, time, attention, people) to one use, you lose the best alternative use. The opportunity cost is the value of the road not taken. Most bad decisions result from ignoring opportunity costs, not from miscalculating direct costs.

steps.description: For the resource being allocated, brainstorm every plausible alternative use. The opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative, not the average of all alternatives.

inputs.name: resource-description
inputs.desc: The resource being allocated (money, time, a person, a machine, attention)

inputs.name: proposed-use
inputs.desc: The use being considered for the resource

inputs.name: resource-amount
inputs.desc: The amount of the resource being allocated

outputs.name: alternative-uses
outputs.desc: Every plausible alternative use for the same resource, with a rough value estimate for each

outputs.name: best-alternative
outputs.desc: The single best alternative use: the one with the highest value

process: List every plausible alternative use for this resource. Include: doing nothing (keeping the resource in reserve), applying it to a different project, investing it, using it to reduce a different risk, using it to seize a different opportunity.
For each alternative, estimate the value it would produce. Use the same metric as the proposed use (dollars, time saved, risk reduced, skills gained).
Identify the best alternative: the one with the highest estimated value. This is the opportunity cost of the proposed use.
The proposed use is only worth it if its value exceeds the best alternative's value. If the best alternative is better, do that instead.

steps.description: Quantify the opportunity cost. Express it in the same units as the direct cost so the two can be added for the true total cost.

outputs.name: true-cost-calculation
outputs.desc: The true cost of the proposed use: direct cost plus opportunity cost (the value of the best alternative foregone)

outputs.name: decision-threshold
outputs.desc: The minimum value the proposed use must produce to be worthwhile: it must exceed the true cost, not just the direct cost

process: Calculate the direct cost of the proposed use: the money spent, the time consumed, the wear on equipment, the attention diverted.
Calculate the opportunity cost: the value the best alternative would have produced. This is the foregone benefit.
Add them: true cost = direct cost + opportunity cost. The proposed use must produce value exceeding this sum to be a rational allocation.
If the proposed use barely exceeds the direct cost but falls short of the true cost, the allocation is destroying value. The resource should go to the best alternative instead.

steps.description: Separate sunk costs from opportunity costs. Sunk costs are already spent and irrelevant to the forward-looking decision. Only future costs and opportunity costs matter.

outputs.name: forward-looking-analysis
outputs.desc: The decision stripped of sunk costs: only future direct costs, future opportunity costs, and future benefits

outputs.name: sunk-cost-inventory
outputs.desc: The sunk costs identified and explicitly excluded from the decision, with the reasoning

process: Identify any costs already incurred: money already spent, time already invested, contracts already signed. These are sunk costs.
Remove them from the analysis. The question is never 'should I have started this?' but 'given where I am now, should I continue?'
Recalculate the forward-looking true cost: remaining direct costs plus the opportunity cost of the remaining resources.

The most common error: continuing a losing investment because 'we have already spent too much to stop.' The sunk cost is gone regardless. The only question is whether the remaining investment produces more than its opportunity cost.

steps.description: Log the decision with the full cost analysis. Review past decisions to calibrate your opportunity cost estimates over time.

outputs.name: decision-record
outputs.desc: The complete decision record: proposed use, best alternative, direct cost, opportunity cost, true cost, expected value, and the decision

outputs.name: review-date
outputs.desc: The date to review the decision and compare the actual outcome to the estimate

process: Record the decision: what was allocated, to what use, what was the best alternative foregone, and what was the estimated true cost.
Record the expected value of the chosen use. This creates a benchmark for the review.
Set the review date: at the point when the value of the chosen use should be measurable (end of the project, end of the quarter, end of the year).
At review: compare actual value to expected value and actual opportunity cost to estimated opportunity cost. Use the data to improve future estimates.

description: Define signals that trigger resource rebalancing instead of rebalancing on a fixed calendar. Calendar-based reviews miss urgency. Signal-based triggers catch problems when they emerge. Works for investment portfolios, marketing budgets, team allocations, and household spending.

steps.description: Define the target allocation and the drift thresholds that trigger rebalancing.

inputs.name: target-allocation
inputs.desc: The intended allocation across categories (e.g., 60/30/10 split, or specific dollar amounts per category)

inputs.name: rebalancing-cost
inputs.desc: The cost of rebalancing (transaction fees, disruption, switching costs)

outputs.name: drift-thresholds
outputs.desc: For each category: the maximum acceptable drift from target before rebalancing triggers (expressed as percentage points or dollar amounts)

outputs.name: monitoring-setup
outputs.desc: How to measure drift: the data source, the measurement frequency, and the alert mechanism

process: Set the target allocation: the intended percentage or amount for each category. This is the baseline.

Calculate the drift threshold for each category. The threshold depends on the rebalancing cost: if rebalancing is cheap (moving money between accounts), set tight thresholds (5 percentage points). If rebalancing is expensive (hiring, restructuring), set wider thresholds (15-20 percentage points).
Define the monitoring: how often is the actual allocation measured, and how is the drift calculated? Automated monitoring is better than manual checks.
Set the alert: when any category drifts beyond its threshold, notify the decision-maker. Do not wait for the next scheduled review.

steps.description: Trigger rebalancing when a category's performance diverges from expectations, even if the allocation has not drifted.

inputs.name: target-allocation
inputs.desc: The target allocation with expected returns

outputs.name: performance-triggers
outputs.desc: For each category: the minimum acceptable performance level and the performance decline that triggers review

outputs.name: combined-trigger-set
outputs.desc: The complete set of triggers: allocation drift and performance divergence, with the response for each

process: For each category, define the expected performance: the return, the output, the conversion rate, or whatever metric measures its value.
Set the performance trigger: a decline of more than 20% from the trailing average, or two consecutive periods below the minimum acceptable level.
When a performance trigger fires, the response is: investigate the cause (is it temporary or structural?), and if structural, reallocate away from the underperforming category.
Combine the drift triggers and performance triggers into a single trigger set. Any trigger that fires initiates a review.

steps.description: Trigger rebalancing when the context changes: a new opportunity emerges, a risk materializes, or the goals change.

outputs.name: context-triggers
outputs.desc: External events that should trigger a rebalancing review: market changes, competitive moves, life events, regulatory changes, new information

outputs.name: full-trigger-framework
outputs.desc: The complete trigger framework: drift, performance, and context, with priority and response for each

process: List the external events that would change the optimal allocation: a new competitor enters the market (reallocate to defense), a new channel opens (reallocate to growth), a life event occurs (reallocate to stability), a regulation changes (reallocate to compliance).
For each context trigger, define the expected allocation change: where should resources move, and by how much?
Combine all three trigger types (drift, performance, context) into a single framework with priorities. Context triggers typically override drift triggers.
The framework replaces the calendar-based review. Rebalancing happens when it is needed, not when a date arrives.

description: Systematically find and eliminate commitments that no longer earn their keep. Subscriptions, projects, relationships, habits, and investments that persist through inertia rather than value. The method: inventory everything, calculate the forward-looking value, and terminate anything where continuing costs more than stopping.

steps.description: Inventory every ongoing commitment: subscriptions, projects, contracts, memberships, recurring meetings, habits, investments being held.

inputs.name: scope
inputs.desc: What to audit (personal finances, business operations, team calendar, project portfolio, investment portfolio)

inputs.name: time-period
inputs.desc: The lookback period for identifying commitments (typically 12 months)

outputs.name: commitment-list
outputs.desc: Every ongoing commitment with: what it is, what it costs per period (in money, time, or attention), when it started, and when it was last evaluated

outputs.name: auto-renewal-flags
outputs.desc: Commitments that auto-renew without active decision, which are the most likely to persist without value

process: Pull every recurring charge from bank and credit card statements. Pull every recurring meeting from the calendar. Pull every active project from the task list. Pull every held investment from the portfolio.
For each, record: the ongoing cost per period (dollars, hours, attention units), when the commitment started, and whether there was an active decision to continue it in the last 12 months.
Flag auto-renewal commitments: subscriptions, memberships, retainers, and recurring meetings that continue unless someone actively cancels them. These are the highest-risk sunk cost traps.
Sort by cost per period, highest first. The most expensive commitments deserve the most scrutiny.

steps.description: For each commitment, assess the forward-looking value. Ignore what you have already spent. Ask only: knowing what I know now, would I start this commitment today?

outputs.name: value-assessments
outputs.desc: Each commitment rated: keep (value exceeds cost), review (value is marginal), or eliminate (cost exceeds value)

outputs.name: elimination-candidates
outputs.desc: Commitments where the forward-looking cost exceeds the forward-looking value

process: For each commitment, answer: if I were not already in this commitment, would I start it today at the current cost? If the answer is no, it is an elimination candidate.
Estimate the forward-looking value: what will this commitment produce in the next 12 months? Be specific. If you cannot name the value, the value is probably zero.
Estimate the forward-looking cost: what will it cost in the next 12 months, including the opportunity cost of the money, time, or attention consumed?

Do not consider the sunk cost. 'We have already invested $50,000 in this project' is irrelevant. The $50,000 is gone regardless of whether you continue. The only question is whether the next dollar is worth it.

steps.description: Terminate the elimination candidates. For each: the termination method, the notice period, and the exit cost.

outputs.name: termination-plan
outputs.desc: For each elimination candidate: the steps to terminate, the notice required, the exit cost (early termination fees, cleanup), and the savings per period after termination

outputs.name: total-savings
outputs.desc: The total resources freed per period by eliminating all candidates

process: For each candidate, determine the termination method: cancel the subscription, close the project, end the contract, sell the investment, decline the recurring meeting.

Calculate the exit cost: early termination fees, cleanup work, transition costs. If the exit cost exceeds the savings for the remaining contract term, it may be cheaper to let the commitment expire naturally.
Execute the terminations in order of savings: the highest-savings candidates first. Each termination frees resources for higher-value uses.
Record the total savings per period. This is the budget freed for reallocation to higher-value commitments.

steps.description: Prevent new sunk cost traps from forming. Every new commitment gets a review date. Every auto-renewal gets a decision checkpoint.

outputs.name: commitment-review-calendar
outputs.desc: A calendar of review dates: every commitment reviewed at least annually, with the review checklist

outputs.name: new-commitment-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for new commitments: every new commitment must have a defined review date, a success metric, and a termination trigger

process: For every surviving commitment, set an annual review date. At the review, re-ask: knowing what I know now, would I start this today?
For every auto-renewal commitment, set a reminder 30 days before renewal. The reminder forces an active decision to continue or cancel.
For every new commitment going forward, require three things before starting: a defined review date, a measurable success metric, and a termination trigger (the condition under which you will stop).
Run the full sunk cost elimination audit annually. Commitments accumulate like barnacles. Regular scraping keeps the hull clean.

description: Calculate how long you can survive at different spending levels. Runway analysis answers the question: if all income stops today, how many months can I sustain operations? Then: what if I cut to 75% spending? 50%? The answers inform every strategic decision. Works for startups, households, nonprofits, and departments.

steps.description: Calculate the total liquid reserves: cash and assets that can be converted to cash within 5 business days without significant loss.

inputs.name: asset-list
inputs.desc: All assets with their type, balance, and liquidity (how quickly can they be converted to cash and at what cost)

inputs.name: credit-facilities
inputs.desc: Available but undrawn credit lines, their limits, and their costs

outputs.name: liquid-reserves
outputs.desc: Total immediately available reserves: cash plus near-cash assets, with the time to access each

outputs.name: extended-reserves
outputs.desc: Total reserves including assets that take 30-90 days to liquidate, minus the expected liquidation discount

process: List every asset. Classify by liquidity: tier 1 (cash, checking, savings, money market: available in 1-2 business days), tier 2 (stocks, bonds, CDs: available in 3-5 business days with potential market loss), tier 3 (real estate, equipment, inventory: 30-90+ days to liquidate with significant discount).
Calculate liquid reserves: tier 1 plus tier 2 minus any locked or restricted funds.
Calculate extended reserves: liquid reserves plus tier 3 minus the estimated liquidation discount (typically 20-40% for fire-sale conditions).
Note available credit lines separately. Credit is not a reserve (it must be repaid with interest), but it extends the runway at a cost.

steps.description: Calculate the monthly burn rate at current spending, 75% spending, and 50% spending. Separate fixed costs (cannot be cut quickly) from variable costs (can be cut immediately).

inputs.name: monthly-expenses
inputs.desc: All monthly expenses, categorized as fixed (contractual, cannot be reduced in under 90 days) or variable (can be reduced or eliminated within 30 days)

outputs.name: burn-rate-scenarios
outputs.desc: Monthly burn rate at three levels: current (100%), reduced (75% of variable costs cut), and survival (50% of variable costs cut plus all discretionary eliminated)

outputs.name: minimum-viable-spend
outputs.desc: The absolute minimum monthly spend to keep the operation alive: only fixed obligations plus the bare minimum variable costs

process: Separate fixed costs (rent, loan payments, insurance, contractual salaries) from variable costs (marketing, discretionary spending, travel, subscriptions, overtime, temporary staff).
Current burn rate: all fixed plus all variable.
Reduced burn rate (75%): all fixed plus 75% of variable (cut the lowest-value 25% of variable spending).
Survival burn rate (50%): all fixed plus 50% of variable (cut everything that does not directly generate revenue or keep the lights on).
Minimum viable spend: only the costs that, if not paid, would cause legal default, loss of the facility, or inability to operate at all.

steps.description: Calculate the runway in months at each spending level. Runway = liquid reserves divided by monthly burn rate.

inputs.name: burn-rate-scenarios
inputs.desc: The burn rates at each spending level

outputs.name: runway-table
outputs.desc: Runway in months at each spending level: current, reduced, survival, and minimum viable

outputs.name: runway-danger-zones
outputs.desc: The dates when each runway expires, and the decision points (e.g., at 6 months runway, trigger reduced spending; at 3 months, trigger survival mode)

process: Calculate: runway at current burn = liquid reserves divided by current monthly burn. Repeat for reduced, survival, and minimum viable.
If any remaining income is expected (even reduced), subtract it from the burn rate before dividing. Runway with partial income is longer than zero-income runway.

Define the danger zones: less than 12 months runway at current burn triggers planning. Less than 6 months triggers reduced spending. Less than 3 months triggers survival mode. Less than 1 month is a crisis.
Convert to calendar dates. 'We have 8 months of runway at current burn' becomes 'we run out on [specific date].' Dates create urgency; months create abstraction.

steps.description: Plan the actions that extend the runway at each danger zone. Decisions made before the danger zone are better than decisions made during it.

inputs.name: runway-danger-zones
inputs.desc: The danger zone thresholds and dates

outputs.name: extension-actions
outputs.desc: For each danger zone: the specific spending cuts, revenue acceleration, and asset liquidation actions that extend the runway, with the months gained from each

outputs.name: runway-monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: The monthly runway recalculation schedule with the data inputs and the escalation path when a danger zone is approaching

process: At the 12-month threshold: identify the variable costs with the lowest return. Reduce or eliminate them. Accelerate revenue: invoice faster, collect receivables, offer prepayment discounts.
At the 6-month threshold: cut all non-essential variable costs. Reduce headcount if applicable. Liquidate tier 2 assets. Activate credit lines if the cost is acceptable.
At the 3-month threshold: survival mode. Only minimum viable spend. Liquidate tier 3 assets. Negotiate payment deferrals with creditors. Explore emergency financing.

Recalculate the runway monthly. After each action, update the reserves and burn rate. The runway should be extending, not shrinking. If it is shrinking despite cuts, the revenue problem is structural.
